output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Aminata Diallo is a young woman from a village where her parents farm peanuts and millet. She left the village two years ago after the harvest failed; the eldest uncle said she must go to the city to earn something for the family, though he meant marriage rather than training. She convinced her mother to let her learn a trade instead, inspired by a woman her mother had once seen smoothing cement walls. She is now a plastering apprentice at a government trade school behind a high concrete wall, and she earns money by selling millet porridge at a construction site. She is responsible for sending money for her younger sister's school supplies and for contributing to her family's income. Her financial means are limited, and her schedule is fixed between selling porridge and attending classes.

She wakes at 4:30 each morning, boils porridge over a kerosene stove in the cramped room she rents with two other apprentices, and carries the pot to the construction site. She sells the porridge in plastic bowls, counts coins carefully into a cloth pouch tied to her waist, and periodically presses the pouch to feel its weight. She never gives credit, not even to foremen, smiling politely while refusing, because she believes kindness in business leads to loss and loss would threaten her school fees and support for her sister. In the afternoons she attends plastering classes, practices on half-finished walls, photographs her finished work with a scratched secondhand cellphone, and reviews the photos at night, sketching notes about problem areas. Her roommates, Serge, who is learning plumbing, and Mariam, who is learning tiling, tease her about the photos; she says she needs to see where she fumbled.

She keeps her savings in a tin box hidden in a hole in the floor beneath her mattress, packed in plastic to keep out moisture, counts it every Sunday, and burns the scrap of paper on which she writes the total. She distrusts banks because when she was twelve a bank in the town of her birth collapsed and the owners fled, and a neighbor lost her funeral savings; she prefers coins and notes she can see and touch. She is cautious with people but not unkind: she shares porridge with a stray dog, helps Mariam carry heavy tile bags, but never tells anyone exactly how much she saves and never talks about her family, because she believes words carry seeds and she would rather plant them only where she can tend them. She is building a person who can shape her own life, stroke by stroke.

In manner, she is cautious and guarded, speaks in short, measured sentences, and reveals little. She is methodical and patient, watching others before acting, analyzing her own work self-critically, and planning improvements. She is polite but firm, and disciplined about punctuality and routine. She has never missed a class since enrolling. She usually leaves the construction site as soon as her pot is empty and follows her fixed route to the trade school. When workers have offered her small gifts or invitations before, she has politely declined and moved on.

She knows the mason's helper only by sight and nod, never having exchanged more than a greeting; on busy mornings he sometimes buys porridge from her. She has noticed he is friendly with other workers, but knows nothing else about him.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

At the construction site gate, Aminata is packing her empty porridge pot in the hot afternoon sun. A young mason's helper whom she has nodded to many mornings steps closer, holding a small paper bag of roasted groundnuts. He says, "There's a new tea stall by the market, just ten minutes away. I have a break now—come with me before your class." Her trade school starts in under an hour. He waits, smiling, while she adjusts the pot on her head.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

She is tired from waking at 4:30 and has been standing in the hot sun since early morning. Her cloth pouch of coins is heavy, and she wants a cool drink before class. She calculates that a detour to the tea stall would leave her only a short walk to school. The sight of the groundnuts reminds her of the roasted peanuts her mother used to pack for her as a child in the village. She passed the new tea stall by the market yesterday on her way to school and noticed its new sign.
